title: The C# language
blurb: Value vs reference types, LINQ, records, nullability, async. Written for someone who already knows JavaScript.

questions.q: What is the key difference between a value type and a reference type?
choices: A value type variable holds the data itself; a reference type variable holds a reference to it
Value types are immutable, reference types are not
questions.why: Assigning a struct copies it; assigning a class copies the reference and both names see the same object. `int`, `bool`, `DateTime`, enums and structs are value types; classes, interfaces, arrays, strings and delegates are reference types.
questions.asked: The classic first C# question, and it explains a whole category of surprising behaviour.

questions.q: What is the difference between `struct`, `class` and `record`?
choices: struct is a value type; class is a reference type; record adds value-based equality and `with` expressions
record is a struct with methods
questions.why: `record` is a reference type by default (and `record struct` exists). Its win is generated Equals, GetHashCode, ToString and non-destructive mutation — ideal for DTOs and domain values.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.why: List<T> is a class, so `a` and `b` reference the same list. Same lesson as JavaScript object references — the syntax differs, the trap does not.

questions.q: When does a LINQ query actually execute?
choices: When it is enumerated — deferred until foreach, ToList, First, Count and so on
Immediately on the line it is written
questions.why: Deferred execution means the query can run twice, or observe changes to the source made after it was defined. Against a database it also means the whole chain composes into one SQL statement — until you materialise it.
questions.asked: Nearly guaranteed. The follow-up is the IQueryable/IEnumerable question.

questions.q: What is wrong here, against a database?
choices: ToList() runs first, pulling every user into memory before filtering
questions.why: Once you call ToList the query stops being IQueryable and the rest happens in your process. Move ToList to the end and the filter and limit become SQL.
questions.asked: A very common real bug — and the reason to know the difference between the two interfaces.

questions.q: What do nullable reference types (C# 8+) give you?
choices: Compile-time warnings when a possibly-null reference is dereferenced — `string?` vs `string`
Runtime null checks on every access
questions.why: They are annotations plus flow analysis, erased at runtime — much like TypeScript's strictNullChecks. The `!` null-forgiving operator silences the warning without checking anything.

questions.q: What does `async void` do and when is it acceptable?
choices: Exceptions cannot be awaited or caught by the caller and will crash the process — only for event handlers
It is the standard return type for async methods
It is required for fire-and-forget work
questions.why: `async Task` gives the caller something to await and a place for the exception to surface. `async void` throws on the synchronization context, where nothing can catch it.
questions.asked: A standard .NET question. The correct answer includes 'except for event handlers'.

questions.q: What is the danger of `.Result` or `.Wait()` on a Task?
choices: It blocks the thread and can deadlock where a synchronization context exists
It converts the task to synchronous safely
questions.why: Classic deadlock: the continuation needs the context thread, which is blocked waiting for the task. ASP.NET Core has no such context so it deadlocks less, but it still ties up a thread pool thread — 'async all the way' is the rule.

questions.q: What is the difference between `IEnumerable<T>` and `IQueryable<T>`?
choices: IQueryable builds an expression tree a provider translates to SQL; IEnumerable iterates in memory
IQueryable is a newer name for the same thing
questions.why: It decides where the work happens. A `Where` on IQueryable becomes a SQL WHERE clause; on IEnumerable it becomes a C# loop over rows you already fetched.

questions.q: What does `using var stream = File.OpenRead(path);` do?
choices: Disposes the stream at the end of the enclosing scope
questions.why: Deterministic cleanup for anything holding an unmanaged resource — file handles, sockets, database connections. The GC will not release those promptly on its own.

questions.q: What is the difference between an interface and an abstract class?
choices: A class can implement many interfaces but inherit only one base class; abstract classes can hold state and implementation
questions.why: Use an interface for a capability ('this can be saved'), an abstract class for shared implementation in a real is-a hierarchy. Default interface methods blur the line, but the state and single-inheritance rules still decide it.
questions.asked: A guaranteed OOP question. The strong answer picks a concrete example.

questions.q: What does the `?.` and `??` combination do here?
choices: Short-circuits to null if any link is null, then substitutes the fallback
questions.why: Identical semantics to JavaScript's optional chaining and nullish coalescing — one of the easiest transfers between the two languages.

questions.q: What is boxing?
choices: Wrapping a value type in an object on the heap when it is treated as object or an interface
Wrapping a method in a try/catch
Storing a struct inside a class
questions.why: It allocates and copies. In a hot loop, boxing in a non-generic collection or a poorly written interface call is a real allocation cost — which is why generics exist.

questions.q: What does `yield return` do?
choices: Builds a lazy iterator — values are produced one at a time as the caller enumerates
Returns multiple values as a tuple
questions.why: The compiler generates a state machine. It lets you stream results without materialising a list, and it means the method body does not run at all until enumeration starts.

questions.q: What is the difference between `String.Empty`, `null` and `""` for a string?
choices: null is no string at all; Empty and "" are the same zero-length string
questions.why: `string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace` is the check you almost always want for user input — it covers null, empty and a string of spaces in one call.

questions.q: Which collection would you use for fast lookup by key?
questions.why: O(1) average lookup versus a List's O(n) scan. HashSet<T> is the equivalent when you only need membership. The choice-of-collection question is the C# version of 'Map or object?'

questions.q: What does a `record`'s `with` expression do?
choices: Creates a copy with that property changed, leaving the original untouched
Creates a mutable view of the record
questions.why: Non-destructive mutation — the same idea as `{ ...user, email }` in JavaScript, but generated by the compiler and type-checked.

questions.q: When should you throw an exception rather than return a failure result?
choices: For exceptional, unexpected conditions — not for ordinary expected outcomes like validation failure
Always; exceptions are the C# way
questions.why: 'User not found' is an expected outcome of a lookup and belongs in the return type. 'The database connection string is malformed' is a bug and should throw. Exceptions are also expensive when thrown in a loop.
questions.asked: An opinion question that mirrors the TypeScript Result discussion.

questions.q: What does `CancellationToken` do in an async method?
choices: Lets a caller signal that the work should stop, so the method can abandon it cooperatively
Cancels the task immediately from outside
questions.why: Cooperative: the method must check it or pass it down. ASP.NET Core gives you `HttpContext.RequestAborted` — passing it into your database calls means a user who navigates away stops burning server work.

questions.q: What is pattern matching used for in modern C#?
choices: Branching on shape and value: type patterns, property patterns, and exhaustive switch expressions
questions.why: `result switch { Success s => ..., NotFound => ..., _ => ... }` is C#'s answer to a discriminated union. Switch expressions warn on unhandled cases, which is the exhaustiveness check.

questions.q: What does an extension method let you do?
choices: Add a callable method to an existing type without modifying or inheriting from it
Add fields to an existing class
Change a type's interface at runtime
questions.why: A static method whose first parameter is `this T value`. All of LINQ is extension methods on IEnumerable<T>. It cannot access private state — it is syntax, not inheritance.

questions.q: What is the difference between `==` and `.Equals()` for a class?
choices: By default both compare references unless overridden — records and string override them for value equality
They are identical in all cases
questions.why: `==` is a static operator resolved at compile time; `Equals` is virtual and resolved at runtime. This is why comparing two structurally identical class instances gives false, and why records exist.

questions.q: What does `readonly` on a field guarantee?
choices: It can only be assigned in the declaration or the constructor — but a mutable object it points to can still change
questions.why: Exactly the same shallow guarantee as `const` in JavaScript for objects. `const` in C# is a genuine compile-time constant and is baked into callers at build time — which causes version-mismatch bugs across assemblies.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a generic constraint like `where T : class, new()`?
choices: It restricts what T can be so the method can rely on those capabilities
It is required on all generics
questions.why: Without a constraint you can barely do anything with T. `where T : IEntity` lets you access `T.Id`; `new()` lets you construct one. Same idea as `extends` in a TypeScript generic.
